Case Information: The patient is a 37-year-old male from a non-consanguineous Chinese family. At age 35, he began to experience progressive weakness in his hands, with a notable reduction in grip strength, particularly in the right hand. Six months later, muscle atrophy and fibrillation were observed in his hands, leading to an inability to hold objects or write. One year later, he developed weakness in his lower extremities without sensory disturbances. He currently has difficulty climbing stairs, standing up from a squatting position, lifting his foot upward, and frequently trips. Physical examination showed normal cranial nerves and no orolingual fasciculations or atrophy. Neck flexion strength was rated 5 on the MRC muscle scale (grades 0–5). Muscle strength on both sides was as follows: triceps and biceps 3/3, forearm flexors 2/2, intrinsic hand muscles 1/1, iliopsoas muscles 4/4, quadriceps muscles 3/3, tibialis anterior and gastrocnemius muscles 2/2. Deep tendon reflexes were absent. There were no sensory abnormalities or coordination difficulties in any limbs. Muscle atrophy was prominent, especially in the interosseous muscles of the hands, bilateral gastrocnemius, and anterior tibial muscles. Muscle fibrillation was noted in the biceps and quadriceps muscles. Serum creatine kinase level was 668 U/L (normal range: 50–310 U/L). Tests for extractable nuclear antigens were negative, and serum sex hormone levels were normal. Peripheral neuropathy antibodies, including GM1-antibody and GQ1b-antibody, were negative, and cerebrospinal fluid showed no albuminocytological dissociation. Nerve conduction studies revealed severe reductions in compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes and motor conduction velocities in the bilateral median, ulnar, and radial nerves, with normal sensory conduction. Right ulnar nerve F-waves were absent. Electromyogram (EMG) showed chronic denervation/reinnervation (e.g., motor unit action potentials of increased amplitude and duration, with reduced interference patterns) in three regions, including the bilateral extremities and sternocleidomastoid muscles, along with spontaneous activity (positive sharp waves). Echocardiography and electrocardiogram evaluations showed no cardiac abnormalities. Lower limb muscle MRI indicated significant involvement of the gastrocnemius muscle at the calf level, with a strongly increased signal intensity in turbo inversion recovery magnitude (TIRM) sequences, suggesting muscular edema. Mild signal intensity increases in the soleus and tibialis anterior muscles were observed in the T2 sequence, indicating fat replacement. Slight fatty degeneration was detected in the posterior compartment of the proximal leg, including the semimembranosus and semitendinosus muscles.
Diagnostic Tests: Next-generation sequencing identified a heterozygous missense mutation (c.7123G > A, p.V2375I) in the Ig-like domain 21 of FLNC. Confirmation of the variant was undertaken by Sanger sequencing using an ABI 3730XL DNA Sequencer. The mutation was absent in the DNA of 100 healthy unrelated controls, and the allele frequency in the Asian population is zero according to the Exome Aggregation Consortium. The p.V2375I missense mutation affects valine at position 2375, which is highly conserved from mice to humans.

Case Information: The patient is a 6-month-old male child born to a non-consanguineous, phenotypically normal couple. He was delivered at 39 weeks of gestation via cesarean section with a birth weight of 2,820 grams. At 6 months, his weight was 5.6 kg (<3rd percentile), his height was 63 cm (<3rd percentile), and his head circumference was 46 cm (90th percentile). The patient exhibited poor growth and developmental delays, including the absence of social smiling and maternal recognition by 12 months of age. Mild dysmorphic features were noted. Echocardiography, electromyography, hematological and biochemical tests for renal and liver function were normal, and screening for inborn errors of metabolism showed no abnormalities.
Diagnostic Tests: Conventional cytogenetic analysis of the proband revealed an abnormal male karyotype, 46,XY,der(11)t(1;11)(q41;p15.5). The array CGH for the proband revealed that the breakpoint of a contiguous duplication on the long arm of chromosome 1 was located in 1q41 band. We also observed two BAC clone deletions on the short arm (11p15.5) of chromosome 11. FISH analysis confirmed the breakpoint of a contiguous duplication on the long arm of chromosome 1 was located between BAC_4527 and BAC_7952. The skipped duplication pattern by the array CGH around at 1q43 region was proved to be false by FISH with 1q43 probe. The deletion of 11p15.5 predicted by the array CGH was also confirmed by FISH.

Case Information: A 24-year-old male visited the dermatology outpatient department with lifelong thickening of the skin on his palms and soles, which had progressively spread to the backs of his hands and feet over the past 5 years. He reported recurrent blistering and painful cracks on his palms. For the past 6 months, he had hyperpigmented, raised, scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of both knees and elbows. Additionally, he experienced redness and mildly painful fissures at the corners of his mouth for the same duration. He had no other systemic issues and no family history of similar symptoms. On physical examination, there was widespread thickening of the skin on the palms and soles, extending to the backs of the hands and feet, with irregular, poorly defined borders and prominent knuckle pads. The skin on the palms and soles appeared thick, waxy, yellowish, and emitted an unpleasant odor, with a loss of normal skin patterns. There were multiple erosions and fissures of varying sizes on both palms, and pitted keratolysis on the soles. The fingers exhibited a pseudosclerodermatous appearance, with some showing conical tapering and digital constrictions at various points, along with mild flexion deformity. The nails were thickened and hypercurved, with dystrophic changes noted in both great toenails. The patient also had multiple hyperkeratotic, scaly, irregular, and poorly defined plaques on the extensor surfaces of both elbows and knees. Additionally, the lower lip was dry, erythematous, and thickened, with angular cheilitis.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathology of palmar skin showed lining of stratified squamous epithelium with hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, and acanthosis. Superficial dermis shows mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates.

Case Information: A 26-year-old otherwise healthy, nulligravida female presented to the emergency department with worsening right lower quadrant pain, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting for four days. She also reported low back discomfort and abdominal discomfort, which she attributed to forceful vomiting. She had taken a muscle relaxant earlier that morning, but the pain in her right lower quadrant persisted. Her primary care physician advised her to go to the emergency department for evaluation. Over the past two years, she had experienced recurrent and increasing abdominal discomfort, increased heartburn, right and left lower quadrant pain with back pain, and fluctuating periods of diarrhea and constipation. She had been seen in the same emergency department 12 months prior and was treated for a urinary tract infection with antibiotics. Over the past 12 months, she had followed up with her primary care physician and various urgent care clinics approximately four times with similar symptoms; no imaging had been performed at any of those visits. Her history included irregular and heavy periods since she was young. Family history was positive for pancreatic, prostate, breast, and throat cancer spanning three generations. The patient had a noticeably tender abdominal examination, but all vital signs were stable. Laboratory data revealed leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 16.4 with a left shift, pyuria, and bacteriuria. The patient was currently being treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Diagnostic Tests: Computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a very large cystic pelvic mass, 35x24 x36cm, extending into the abdomen. The mass displaced bowel loops and the colon and had a thin peripheral rind measuring 5mm. There was also free fluid in the pelvic cavity.

Case Information: A 49-year-old male reported visual impairment in his left eye for over 20 years, which he had previously ignored. He visited the hospital on March 3, 2020, with a primary complaint of visual disturbance in his right eye that began the previous year. Family history revealed no notable abnormalities. At the initial visit, corrected visual acuity was 20/12.5 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were measured at 16 mmHg in the right eye and 14 mmHg in the left eye. Examination showed clear cornea, anterior chamber, and lens. Chorioretinal atrophy with pigmentation along the retinal veins was noted in the right fundus. Autofluorescence imaging showed loss of autofluorescence corresponding to the pigmented area. Extensive changes were observed in the left eye on both the fundus photograph and the autofluorescence fundus photograph. Dynamic quantitative visual field testing identified a scotoma in the right eye corresponding to the area of retinochoroidal atrophy. Visual field constriction was noted in the left eye.
Diagnostic Tests: An electroretinogram test was performed on August 18, 2021, and the waveforms of right and left eye showed an attenuated and negative pattern, respectively.

Case Information: A 39-year-old woman reported experiencing decreased vision in her right eye (OD) for the past year, accompanied by watering and redness in the same eye. She observed an irregular increase in the size of her pupil in OD. There was no history of trauma or previous surgeries. She had been prescribed brimonidine and timolol maleate combination therapy for glaucoma in OD. Upon examination, her visual acuity in OD was 6/12, improving to 6/6 with pinhole, and in her left eye (OS) was 6/6. Intraocular pressure (IOP) measured with Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) was 22 mmHg in OD while on IOP-lowering medication and 12 mmHg in OS. Examination of OD revealed conjunctival congestion, a clear cornea, irregular anterior chamber depth, and shallowness inferiorly. The superior iris appeared stretched with a loss of its normal pattern and exhibited iridodonesis. Ectropion uveae was noted at the inferior pupillary margin, with the posterior pigment epithelium being pulled toward the angle. The pupil was irregular in shape and did not react to light.
Diagnostic Tests: On gonioscopy, her superior angle was open till scleral spur while nasal, inferior, and temporal angles were closed with broad-based PAS.

Case Information: A 38-year-old male patient presented with a long-standing history of multiple non-tender scalp swellings ranging from 2.5 to 3.5 cm in diameter, which have progressively grown over the past year. The skin over the swellings appeared normal. Clinical examination showed multiple nodular lesions coalesced on the anterior region of the scalp, which were solid and movable from the underlying surface. Routine blood investigations were within normal limits. Excisional removal was planned under general anesthesia followed by primary closure.
Diagnostic Tests: The excised specimen showed lobules of epithelial cells arranged in a jigsaw or mosaic pattern. Prominent red basement membrane-like structure encircles the tumor lobules. Each lobule shows a peripheral lining by dark basaloid cells and an inner larger and paler zone of cells.

Case Information: A 16-year-old female presented with thickened skin on the palms and soles, cracked lips, mild scaling on the buttocks, and fissures on the fingers and feet. Additionally, there were erosions on the perianal, vaginal, and nasal mucosa, along with widespread hair loss and sparse hair growth. Nail abnormalities and a hyperkeratotic plaque around the perianal area were also observed. The patient has congenital deafness, delayed speech, and developmental and learning challenges.
Diagnostic Tests: The skin biopsy demonstrated psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with marked hyperkeratosis, and mild acantopapilomatosis, focal porokeratosis, hypergranulosis and superficial perivascular inflammatory infiltration. The immunostaining showed ki67 (mib-1) positive in 45% of the basal cells and CKM (AE1AE3) strongly positive in suprabasal layer.

Case Information: A 54-year-old male was referred to the Rheumatology Division of Fornaroli Hospital from the Infective Department. In February 2014, he was admitted to the hospital due to interstitial lung disease of uncertain origin, presenting with fever accompanied by shivering, dry cough, and chest pain. A chest X-ray revealed a right subclavicle interstitial consolidation. Laboratory tests indicated an ESR of 28 mm/h (cut-off value ≤10 mm/h) and a C-reactive protein level of 6.66 mg/dL (normal range: 0–5). Tests for antinuclear antibodies (ANA), cryoglobulin, extractable nuclear antibodies (ENAs), anti-DNA native antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) were negative. Complement levels (C3, C4) were within the normal range. Rheumatoid factor (RF) was 24 UI/mL (normal range <12) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies were 17 UA/mL (normal range <5). Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels were normal. Quantiferon-TB Gold test was negative. Serology for microbial agents including Legionella, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia was negative. A restrictive defect on functional lung exams was excluded, and the diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) was normal. The patient had no history of smoking.
Diagnostic Tests: A lung/abdominal CT with contrast enhancement showed an interstitial consolidation with centrilobular branching linear structures with bronchial dilatation and multifocal areas of ground-glass attenuation at the right superior and medium lobe of lung in the posterior segment. There were pleura's thickening at the lingula and fibrotic lines with consolidation at the left superior lobe of lung in the anterior segment, also. Moreover, there were some mediastinic bilateral lymphadenopathies. A lung bronchoscopy with a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was made. Bacterial BAL fluid cultures were negative. Culture and genome for Koch's bacillus were negative. BAL cytology excluded monoclonality disorders and showed increased numbers of neutrophils and eosinophils. A positron emission tomography-computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) showed an elevated glucometabolic activity at bilaterally axillary lymphadenopathies and at level of pulmonary consolidation seen at HR-CT. US of right lung, at the fifth posterior intercostal space, showed the presence of Ultrasound Lung Comets (ULCs).

Case Information: A 50-year-old man, with no prior medical history, was admitted to the hospital presenting with shortness of breath and upper abdominal pain. His heart rate was recorded at 130 beats per minute and blood pressure at 110/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed significantly distended jugular veins and a gallop rhythm. A chest X-ray identified pleural effusion, which was confirmed to be exudative through laboratory analysis and showed no abnormal cells. An electrocardiogram indicated sinus tachycardia without changes in the QRS complex, ST segment, or T waves. Spiral CT scan ruled out pulmonary embolism. Echocardiography demonstrated a high cardiac index of 12 L/min/m2, with no signs of pericardial or ventricular dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction of 75%) and no evidence suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis. Cardiac catheterization also indicated a high output cardiac state (12 L/min/m2). Laboratory results showed hemoglobin at 9.8 g/dL, white blood cell count at 18,000/mm3, platelet count at 68,000/mm3, creatinine at 136 µmol/L, calcium serum level at 2.62 mmol/L, and elevated LDH levels.
Diagnostic Tests: Peripheral blood contained 35% of plasma cells. A monoclonal immunoglobulin G (IgG) kappa gammopathy (7.4 g/L) was detected. The percentage of plasma cells in bone marrow analysis was 19%. Chromosome 13 deletion was found on cytogenetic analysis. Immunophenotypic study revealed a CD38, CD138 positive staining, and CD19, CD20 and CD56 negative staining.

Case Information: A 34-year-old female presented with a primary complaint of rapid vision loss in the right eye over three months. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was counting fingers near face in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye. She reported bilateral eye protrusion, more pronounced in the left eye, persisting for 11 years. The patient had a history of primary hyperthyroidism diagnosed at age 22 and was prescribed carbimazole 20 mg twice daily but was non-compliant. Three years later, she noticed neck swelling and increased eye protrusion, more on the left side, which gradually worsened over 12 years. She received intravenous methylprednisolone thrice for increasing proptosis but did not adhere to the treatment regimen. Upon presentation, her BCVA in the right eye had deteriorated from 6/9 to counting fingers near face over three months. Detailed examination revealed that color vision and contrast sensitivity could not be assessed in the right eye due to poor vision, while the left eye had normal color vision and 6% contrast sensitivity. Intraocular pressure (IOP) measured with a Perkins applanation tonometer was 12 mmHg in the right eye and 11 mmHg in the left eye in straight gaze, increasing to 27 mmHg in the right eye and 19 mmHg in the left eye in up gaze. Hertel’s exophthalmometer readings showed 25 mm in the right eye and 27 mm in the left eye, up from previous values of 25 mm and 21 mm, respectively, over the past three months. The palpebral fissure height was 16 mm in the right eye and 18 mm in the left eye. Extra-ocular movements were restricted in all gazes, more so in the right eye. Examination also revealed Mobius sign, Von Graefe’s sign, Dalrymple’s sign, and Enroth sign. The right eye pupil had a sluggish and ill-sustained reaction to light, while the left eye pupil responded briskly. The rest of the anterior segment was unremarkable. The clinical activity score (CAS) was more than four, with eyelid swelling, conjunctival redness, increased proptosis of more than 2 mm, and a decrease in visual acuity of more than 1 Snellen line. Humphrey visual field analysis in the left eye showed peripheral visual field constriction; it was not performed in the right eye due to poor vision.
Diagnostic Tests: The CT scan of the orbit revealed significant changes in muscle thickness of both eyes. The superior rectus muscle of the right eye exhibited a substantial 25% increase from the normal reference range, which was followed by growth in other muscles as follows: the inferior rectus by 19%, the lateral rectus by 15%, and the medial rectus by 11%. Similarly, the left eye displayed a significant 23% enlargement in the inferior rectus, leading to subsequent growth in other muscles as follows: the superior rectus by 18%, the medial rectus by 15%, and the lateral rectus by 12%. Apart from this, both eyes showed hypertrophy of the levator palpebrae superioris and oblique muscles. All the muscles had thickening of the belly with sparing of their tendinous insertions. Also seen was retro-orbital fat stranding.

Case Information: A 10-year-old girl was seen by a neurologist at the OPD Neurology, Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences hospital, Islamabad, for evaluation of congenital microcephaly and seizures. Her family history revealed that her 8-year-old sister exhibited similar characteristics. The patient presented with short stature, a slim body, and distinct facial features including a narrow forehead, bulging eyes, a pointed nose, fuller lips, a broad mouth, and constant drooling. An ophthalmic examination indicated reduced vision due to retinal lesions and bilateral cataracts. She demonstrated good control of her head and other body parts, recognized her parents socially, and was observed smiling. Both children experienced developmental delays, learning disabilities, repetitive behavior, absence of speech, and mood disturbances. The mother reported no viral infections or medication use during the full-term pregnancy, and the delivery was normal.
Diagnostic Tests: The patient had an MRI exam that showed frontal lobe disproportion, cortical simplification, and myelin dystrophy. The results of whole-exome sequencing analysis uncovered that the syndromic MCPH phenotype is due to a missense variant in exon 2 of the RTTN gene (NM_173630.4: c.57G > T(pGlu19Asp). Sanger sequencing data analysis detected the causative variant in the proband and affected sibling as biallelic, while the parents were heterozygous.

Case Information: A 7-year-old boy from southwest China presented with blue cornea, photophobia, and poor vision since birth. At 36 days old, he underwent bilateral anti-glaucoma surgery, followed by long-term use of travoprost and brinzolamide eye drops. Despite this, intraocular pressure remained poorly controlled. The patient also had surgeries for an atrial septal defect and a sublingual cyst. Recently, his eye symptoms worsened, and his vision deteriorated significantly. Consequently, the boy and his family sought medical attention at the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University. A three-generational family pedigree is available.
Diagnostic Tests: Ophthalmic examination of the patient revealed similar pathological changes in both eyes. Uncorrectable poor vision (VOD 0.08, VOS 0.06) and horizontal tremors were observed. No hyperemia or edema was detected in the conjunctiva. The cornea was transparent but the sclera was pale blue. The diameter of the cornea was 14 mm and the center of the anterior chamber was deep. The aqueous humor was clear. The texture of the iris was unclear with partial depigmentation. The lamellar and incomplete disconnections of the root of the iris formed some iridocyridosis and slit-like iris holes (from 4 to 9 o’clock in the right eye, 3 to 9 o’clock in the left eye). The pupil displacement was worse in the right eye. The lens and vitreous of both eyes were slightly turbid. The optic disk was pale, with a cup to disk ratio of 0.9. The retina was ruddy with a wet-silk-like reflection, and the macula was not clear. IOP was 33 mmHg in the right eye and 20 mmHg in the left eye. Binocular B-ultrasound images showed prolongation of the axial axis (27.16 mm in the right eye, 26.56 mm in the left eye) associated with a long period of high IOP. Binocular ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) images showed deepening of the anterior chamber, anterior adhesion, and typical fracture of the iris. The optical coherence tomography (OCT) images of the binocular disk revealed a deepened binocular cup, which was enlarged due to the glaucoma damage.

Case Information: A 47-year-old male presented with abdominal pain persisting for 3 days. He had a history of acute appendicitis 10 years ago, for which he underwent an appendectomy. He had no history of hypertension or diabetes mellitus. The patient was an ex-smoker and a social drinker. It was noted that he consumed raw anchovies 4 days prior to the onset of symptoms. Upon admission, his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse rate 68/min, respiration rate 16/min, and body temperature 37℃. There were no signs of urticaria or facial angioedema. Abdominal examination revealed no splenomegaly or palpable mass, but there was epigastric and periumbilical tenderness without rebound tenderness. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 14.2 g/dL, white blood cell count of 10,350/mm3 with 1.6% eosinophils, platelet count of 221,000/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 4 mm/hr. Blood chemistry results were as follows: total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 29 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 35 IU/L, gamma glutamyl transpeptidase 68 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 138 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase 351 IU/L, blood urea nitrogen 20.2 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 109 mmol/L, amylase 15 IU/L, lipase 32 IU/L, and C-reactive protein 0.34 mg/dL. Urinalysis results were normal.
Diagnostic Tests: The gastroscopic finding showed that there was a marked mucosal swelling and one thread like living worm (about 1.0 to 1.2 cm) was found penetrating the gastric mucosa in the lesser curvature of the lower body. It was withdrawn with biopsy forceps. The endoscopic ultrasonographic finding showed that there was diffuse mucosal and submucosal swelling without mass. The most affected layer was the submucosa. Its character was homogenous and relatively hypodense. The 5-layered wall structure was well preserved. The colonoscopic finding showed that there was round erythematous mucosal swelling and one thread like living structure (about 1.0 to 1.1 cm) was found penetrating the colonic mucosa in the transverse colon area. It was also withdrawn with biopsy forceps. The endoscopic ultrasonographic finding showed that there was diffuse submucosal swelling. Thickened submucosal layer showed generally homogenous echo and was not easily distinguishable from other layers.

Case Information: An 18-year-old female presented with a primary concern of forwardly positioned teeth in the upper front region of the jaw. Family history indicated similar features in her father and grandmother. Extraoral examination showed an upward slant of the eye openings with sparse eyelashes on the lower eyelids. There was underdevelopment of the cheekbones and a small lower jaw. The upper jaw appeared to be protruding, giving the face a distinctive appearance. Intraoral examination found a narrow, high-arched palate. The upper front teeth were angled forward with spacing between the upper and lower front teeth. Root remnants were observed in the positions of teeth 26, 36, and 46. There was generalized gum recession and grade I tooth mobility.
Diagnostic Tests: Radiographs revealed prominent antigonial notch, short ramus, hypoplasia of the mandible, proclined upper anteriors, hypoplasia of zygomatic bone, and maxillary sinus.

Case Information: A 17-year-old girl, born in Italy, with parents who are not related and do not have similar conditions. She is the younger sibling of another case. At birth, she presented with cleft lip and palate, facial abnormalities, foot deformities, and was described as a collodion baby. The initial examination was conducted when she was 3 years old, during which her parents reported allergic reactions affecting her eyes and sensitivity to light. Upon inspection, the palisades of Vogt and meibomian glands were absent. Conjunctival swelling, tear film instability, and a reduced tear meniscus were noted. Annual monitoring of her ocular condition showed stability up to the last visit in March 2023. At that time, mucus secretions in the eyes were observed, and some eyelashes in abnormal positions were removed. The patient uses daily ocular lubricants, anti-inflammatory eyedrops, and lipid-based tear film stabilizers.
Diagnostic Tests: The molecular analysis revealed the presence of the genomic variant 1568T>C (p. Leu523Pro) in exon 13 of TP63, which confirms the L523P mutation in the sterile alpha motif (SAM) domain.

Case Information: A 7-year and 5-month-old Chinese boy, the second child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents, presented with delayed motor development from birth. He achieved head and neck stability at 7 months, rolled over at 11 months, and walked independently at 2 years. His language development was significantly delayed. At 2 years old, he experienced his first epileptic episode, characterized by eye staring, lip cyanosis, foaming at the mouth, and limb jerks, lasting for several minutes. A four-hour sleep-deprived electroencephalogram (EEG) showed continuous spike-and-slow-waves (CSWS). Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and multiple auditory brainstem responses were normal, with no additional abnormalities detected. The seizures ceased spontaneously, and anti-epileptic treatment was initially declined by his parents. However, four months later, the seizures recurred, and valproic acid (VPA) was gradually introduced, starting at 10 mg/kg per day and increasing to 30 mg/kg per day within one month. On a dose of 30 mg/kg per day of VPA, the patient experienced no further seizures. Despite this, he remains unable to care for himself or speak, and neuropsychological testing indicates global intellectual disability and hyperactivity.
Diagnostic Tests: The variant c.625C > T (p.Gln209∗) of CNKSR2 was identified, that was inherited from his unaffected carrier mother. The mutation located toward the N-terminal of the gene alter the codon sequence of the no. 209 amino acid Gln into a termination codon, resulting in a truncated protein lacking the last 825 of 1034 residues, that leads to a truncated protein without the PDZ, DUF1170, PH, and C-terminal ETHV domains.

Case Information: A 19-month-old girl presented with haemolytic anaemia and developmental delay. She was the first child of third-cousin parents, born at 38 weeks following an uncomplicated pregnancy. She was hospitalized in the neonatal intensive care unit for 38 days due to neonatal jaundice and early sepsis, requiring five blood transfusions immediately after birth and an exchange transfusion on the second day of life due to maternal-foetal ABO incompatibility. Another blood transfusion was required at 30 days old for non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. At 9 months, she experienced multiple haemolytic crises triggered by infections and exhibited mild psychomotor developmental delay, unable to sit independently. At 11 months, she was diagnosed with hereditary spherocytosis through a pathologic osmotic fragility test. At 19 months, she was referred with symptoms of an inability to walk and sit without support. Physical examination revealed a weight of 7.3 kg (<3 percentile; z-score −3), height of 78 cm (9th percentile; z-score −1.3), and head circumference of 44.5 cm (5th percentile; z-score −1.6). She exhibited severe malnutrition, paleness, axial hypotonia with muscle bulk loss, and muscle weakness. Decreased deep tendon reflexes, muscle atrophy, and hyperelasticity of the joints were noted in the extremities. Laboratory findings showed severe macrocytic anaemia with haemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, haematocrit 13.1%, mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration 31 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 104 fL, normal white blood cell count 8.868 × 10^9/L, platelet count 95,000/mm3, elevated total bilirubin 24.63 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 18.58 mg/dL. Plasma amino acids, very long-chain fatty acids, serum transferrin isoelectric focusing, and urine organic acids with GCMS were unremarkable. The acylcarnitine profile by MSMS showed normal C0 (62.8 µmol/L, normal range: 10–90 µmol/L) and elevated C3 (7.1 µmol/L, normal range: 0–4.9 µmol/L), with negative methylmalonic acid in the urine by GCMS. Plasma vitamin B12, folic acid, and homocysteine levels were normal. Bone marrow aspiration was normocellular. Ophthalmologic fundus examination, brain stem electric response audiometry (BERA), electromyography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging were all normal. No epileptic activity was observed in the electroencephalography. Muscle biopsy indicated myopathy. During follow-up, the patient required multiple hospitalizations due to haemolytic crises, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and gastroenteritis. At 3 years old, she was admitted to the intensive care unit for pneumonia, required a tracheostomy, and lost most of her acquired developmental milestones.
Diagnostic Tests: Molecular analysis using next-generation sequencing disclosed a p.E105D (c.315G>C) homozygous mutation in the TPI1 gene.

Case Information: A 10-month-old male of Indian descent with a history of atopic dermatitis and egg allergy presented to the outpatient clinic with rhinorrhea and decreased oral intake. His birth history was unremarkable, and immunizations were current. He was initially treated for an upper respiratory infection. Two days later, he returned with additional symptoms including diffuse facial swelling and redness, perioral skin irritation, and right-sided ear pain. Augmentin was prescribed for right-sided otitis media, and topical mupirocin was applied to crusted skin on the right side of his face and upper right perioral region. Rapid COVID-19 and Influenza A and B tests were negative. Due to concerns about a possible allergic reaction, parents were advised to administer an antihistamine and monitor the facial swelling, with instructions to return if symptoms did not improve. That evening, the patient developed a fever of 100.4 °F and was taken to the emergency department at a local children's hospital. The parents were advised to continue the current treatment regimen. Over the next 48 hours, the patient's facial swelling worsened, and he developed swelling in both extremities and widespread skin peeling. Upon returning to the emergency department, initial vital signs showed a heart rate of 137 and a blood pressure of 136/108.
Diagnostic Tests: A physical exam was remarkable for a blanching, peeling, erythematous rash on the face and creases of bilateral arms, legs, and groin. A positive Nikolsky sign was reported.

Case Information: An 8-month-old boy, born to consanguineous parents, presented with persistent seizures and significant developmental delays. Physical examination revealed a small head size with overlapping sutures, a small jaw, a large right ear, and a narrow forehead. Eye examination showed dislocated lenses. Brain ultrasound indicated widespread brain tissue loss, mild softening of brain tissue, and enlarged brain ventricles.
Diagnostic Tests: Uric acid results demonstrated a hypouricaemic hypouricosuric pattern. Sulfocysteine, xanthine and hypoxanthine were elevated in urine.
